children: Congress is moving to restore expanded access to a popular bankruptcy option for small businesses, with the US House of Representatives and Senate both passing bills to restore the program's debt-eligibility limit to $7.5 million after the higher threshold expired in 2024.

The House bill that passed Wednesday would more than double the current debt limit for Subchapter V bankruptcies, which are cheaper and faster than typical Chapter 11 bankruptcies. The Senate version passed unanimously in August, and both bills had broad bipartisan support from Republican and Democratic lawmakers.

The House and Senate have nearly identical substantive provisions, but both chambers of Congress will need to approve the same final text before they send it to the president for his signature, the American Bankruptcy Institute said Thursday.
"Congress is helping more debtors pursue efficient, cost-effective reorganizations while preserving value for all stakeholders," ABI Executive Director Amy Quackenboss said in a statement.

Subchapter V has become a popular way for small businesses to shed debts without losing ownership of their companies and without some of the procedural oversight mechanisms that can add cost and delay in a typical Chapter 11 case.

Unlike a large business bankruptcy case, small businesses can reorganize using Subchapter V without paying for a court-appointed creditors' committee, paying quarterly fees to the US Department of Justice's bankruptcy watchdog, and soliciting creditor votes on a bankruptcy restructuring plan.
Subchapter V filings represented 44% of all Chapter 11 filings in 2023, the year before the debt limit tightened up, according to ABI.

The program has been increasingly popular, even with the dip in eligibility, according to Epiq, which tracks bankruptcy statistics. Over 6,600 businesses filed for Subchapter V bankruptcy from January 2024 to August 2026, and the number of monthly filings increased by 89.9% over that same period.

Subchapter V was initially open to businesses that had up to $2.7 million in debts, but the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act, passed in 2020 to provide emergency assistance to people and businesses affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, temporarily raised the debt threshold to $7.5 million.
The authority for the higher debt limit expired in 2024, reverting the eligibility threshold to the original level, with adjustments for inflation over time.
More than one quarter of Subchapter V debtors that filed from February 2020 to September 2023 would not have qualified for the program under the initial $2.7 million debt threshold, according to ABI.
